mainTopic: The סוטה's punishment מידה כנגד מידה, and how and when the הקב"ה punishes nations, kings and individuals.
overview: This amud finishes a list showing that the סוטה is punished מידה כנגד מידה: every part of her sin is matched by a part of her punishment, on her body and in the ceremony. She sinned in secret, so the הקב"ה brings her sin into the open, and two different פסוקים are brought for this. The גמרא then asks why three separate פסוקים about punishment are needed, and explains what each one adds. The last of them leads to רב חיננא בר פפא's rule that a nation is punished only when it is sent away. רבא's teaching about Egypt's three cups clashes with that rule, so the rule is reworded to be about a king. אמימר gives another version: the הקב"ה strikes a nation once, but בני ישראל survive many blows. Next come רב המנונא's teaching that a person is punished only when his measure is full, and רב חיננא בר פפא's teaching that enemies never captured the works of משה and דוד. The amud ends by returning to the סוטה: whoever wants what is not his loses even what he has.

steps.title: Face, eyes, hair and finger: the punishment matches the sin
steps.stepSummary: The list of מידה כנגד מידה continues. Her face, eyes, hair and fingers are each punished for how she used them to attract her lover.
steps.simpleTranslation: [She made up her face for him, therefore] her face turns pale. She painted her eyes for him, therefore her eyes bulge. She braided her hair for him, therefore the כהן undoes her hair. She signaled to him with her finger, therefore her fingernails fall off.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues a list it already started, showing how each thing the סוטה did for her lover is matched by a punishment on the same part of her body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every line has two halves: what she did ('היא...') and what happens because of it ('לפיכך...'). Some punishments come from drinking the מים המרים, like her face, eyes and nails. Others are done by the כהן during the ceremony, like undoing her hair. The point is that her punishment is not random. It is shaped exactly like her sin.

keyTerms.meaning: Measure for measure: the punishment mirrors the sin
She painted (her eyes) with eye makeup

steps.confusionAlert: The very first words, 'פניה מוריקות', are the end of a sentence that began before this section. Don't read them as a new idea standing alone.

phrases.english: her face turns pale.
phrases.notes: This finishes a line from just before: 'She made up her face for him, therefore...'

phrases.english: She painted her eyes for him;
therefore her eyes bulge.
She braided her hair for him;
therefore a priest undoes her hair.
She signaled to him with a finger;
therefore her fingernails fall off.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִיא כָּחֲלָה לוֹ עֵינֶיהָ — לְפִיכָךְ עֵינֶיהָ בּוֹלְטוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the measure-for-measure list that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each sin of the סוטה with her face, eyes, hair and finger is paid back on that same feature.

steps.title: The belt and the thigh
steps.stepSummary: Two more pairs: her decorative belt is matched by a rough rope the כהן ties on her, and the thigh she offered is the thigh that falls.
steps.simpleTranslation: She tied on a fancy ribbon belt for him, therefore the כהן brings an Egyptian rope and ties it above her chest. She stretched out her thigh for him, therefore her thigh falls away.
steps.whatsHappening: The list keeps going with the same pattern, now about her belt and her thigh.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pretty ribbon worn to attract is replaced by a plain, rough rope. That is a public sign of shame instead of beauty. The thigh falling matches the פסוק's own wording of the סוטה's punishment, so the list ties the curse in the תורה to her actual sin.

keyTerms.meaning: A decorative ribbon or sash worn as a belt

phrases.english: She girded herself for him with a ribbon;
therefore a priest brings an Egyptian rope
and ties it on her above her breasts.
She extended her thigh for him;
therefore her thigh falls away.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִיא חָגְרָה לוֹ בְּצִילְצוֹל — לְפִיכָךְ כֹּהֵן מֵבִיא חֶבֶל הַמִּצְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more items to the same list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Her belt and thigh are punished to match how she used them.

steps.title: Her stomach, her קרבן, and the cup she drinks from
steps.stepSummary: The list ends with three pairs: her stomach swells, her קרבן is animal food, and she drinks bitter water from a cheap clay cup.
steps.simpleTranslation: She received him on her stomach, therefore her stomach swells. She fed him the finest delicacies, therefore her קרבן is animal food. She gave him fine wine to drink in fine cups, therefore the כהן makes her drink the bitter water in a cheap clay cup.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the list. These last pairs move from her body to the food and drink involved in the ceremony.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These pairs show that even the details of the ceremony are part of the message. Fancy food is matched by a קרבן of animal feed. Fine wine in fine cups is matched by bitter water in a plain clay vessel. The luxury she gave her lover is turned into lowliness for her.

keyTerms.meaning: The bitter water the סוטה drinks

steps.whatToRemember: The whole list teaches one idea: every part of the סוטה's sin is mirrored by a part of her punishment, both on her body and in the ceremony itself.

phrases.english: She received him upon her stomach;
therefore her stomach swells.
She fed him the delicacies of the world;
therefore her offering is animal food.
She gave him fine wine to drink
in fine cups;
therefore a priest gives her the bitter water to drink
in an earthenware cup.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִיא קִיבְּלַתּוּ עַל כְּרֵיסָהּ — לְפִיכָךְ בִּטְנָהּ צָבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the list of measure-for-measure pairs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Her stomach, her קרבן and her drinking cup all mirror her sin.

steps.title: She sinned in secret, so the Hidden One turns to face her
steps.stepSummary: The big principle: she hid her sin, so the הקב"ה, called 'the One Who dwells in secret,' turns His attention to her. This is proven from a פסוק in איוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: She acted in secret, so 'the One Who dwells in the secret place of the Most High' sets His face against her, as it says: 'The eye of the adulterer waits for twilight, saying: No eye will see me, and He hides His face' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: After the detailed list, the גמרא gives the overall idea: secret sin is answered by the הקב"ה, Who is Himself hidden, and it brings a פסוק to support this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even here the punishment matches the sin. She acted in hiding, so the One described as 'in hiding' deals with her. The פסוק in איוב describes an adulterer waiting for darkness so no one will see. Its ending, which the גמרא leaves under 'וגו׳', speaks of a hidden face, and that is the proof.

keyTerms.meaning: The One Who dwells in the secret place of the Most High (the הקב"ה)
Sets His face against her / turns His attention to her

phrases.english: She acted in secret;
"He Who dwells in the secret place of the Most High"
phrases.notes: תהלים 91:1. This means הקב"ה.

phrases.english: sets His face against her,
as it is said:
"The eye of the adulterer waits for twilight,
saying: No eye shall see me," and so on.
phrases.notes: איוב 24:15. The 'and so on' hides the key words: 'וסתר פנים ישים', 'and He sets a hidden face'.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִיא עָשְׂתָה בַּסֵּתֶר — יוֹשֵׁב בְּסֵתֶר עֶלְיוֹן שָׂם בָּהּ פָּנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the detailed list to the overall principle behind it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Secret sin is answered by the hidden הקב"ה, proven from איוב 24:15.

steps.title: Another reading: what was hidden becomes public
steps.stepSummary: A second explanation: she sinned in secret, so the הקב"ה made it public, proven from a פסוק in משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: She acted in secret, so the הקב"ה made it known in the open, as it says: 'Though his hatred is hidden by deceit, his evil will be revealed before the congregation.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second way to explain the same idea, with a different פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first explanation stressed who deals with her: the Hidden One. This one stresses the result: hidden sin ends up exposed in front of everyone, just as the סוטה is shamed publicly in the בית המקדש. The פסוק in משלי says this directly.

keyTerms.meaning: The Omnipresent (a name for the הקב"ה)

steps.whatToRemember: Both explanations agree: a sin done in hiding does not stay hidden. The הקב"ה brings it into the open.

phrases.english: Another explanation:
She acted in secret;
the Omnipresent made it known in the open,
as it is said:
"Though hatred is covered by deceit,
his evil will be revealed before the congregation."
phrases.notes: משלי 26:26. Some versions don't have the word in round brackets, 'and so on'.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר: הִיא עָשְׂתָה בַּסֵּתֶר — הַמָּקוֹם פִּירְסְמָה בַּגָּלוּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second explanation and a different פסוק for the same principle.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hidden sin is exposed publicly by the הקב"ה, proven from משלי 26:26.

steps.title: Why do we need the boot verse?
steps.stepSummary: The small sins already add up from the קהלת verse, so why also quote 'every boot stamped with fierceness'?
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he already learns that small sins add up from 'one to one, to find the account,' why do I need the verse 'for every boot stamped with fierceness'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needs a second פסוק when the first one already taught the point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse in קהלת already teaches that small sins combine into one big bill. So the verse in ישעיהו 9:4 looks extra. The גמרא assumes every פסוק must teach something new, and it is setting up an answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Since he already derives it (from another source)
Why do I need it? (asking why a source looks extra)
An account or total, here the total of a person's sins

phrases.english: And since he derives it
from "adding one thing to another, to find the account"
phrases.notes: קהלת 7:27. Here it means small sins add up to one big total.

phrases.english: "For every boot stamped with fierceness"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 9:4

phrases.english: why do I need it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמֵאַחַר דְּנָפְקָא לֵיהּ מֵאַחַת לְאַחַת לִמְצֹא חֶשְׁבּוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new discussion about the ברייתא's verses on how punishment is collected.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the verse 'every boot stamped with fierceness' add beyond the קהלת verse?

steps.title: The boot verse teaches matching measure
steps.stepSummary: The verse teaches that punishment comes in the same measure as the sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed to teach 'by the measure': punishment matches the sin.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the boot verse teaches something new: the punishment fits the size and type of the sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קהלת verse only teaches that small sins add up. The boot verse adds how they are paid back: in a matching measure. So both verses are needed.

keyTerms.meaning: To teach 'by the measure': the punishment fits the sin

phrases.english: To teach that it is by the measure.
phrases.notes: The punishment comes in the same measure as the sin.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The boot verse teaches that punishment matches the measure of the sin.

steps.title: Why do we need the 'full measure' verse?
steps.stepSummary: The boot verse already teaches matching measure, so why also quote 'in full measure, when you send her away'?
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he learns this from 'for every boot stamped with fierceness,' why do I need 'in full measure, when you send her away, you contend with her'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same kind of question again, now about the third פסוק. It is setting up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea of measure-for-measure punishment is already covered by the boot verse. So the verse in ישעיהו 27:8, which also talks about a 'measure,' looks extra.

keyTerms.meaning: In full measure (from the word סְאָה, a unit of measure)

phrases.english: And since he derives it
from "for every boot stamped with fierceness"
"In full measure, when you send her away, you contend with her"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 27:8

phrases.english: why do I need it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמֵאַחַר דְּנָפְקָא לֵיהּ מִכִּי כׇל סְאוֹן סֹאֵן בְּרַעַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the same 'why do I need it' pattern for the next verse.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the 'full measure' verse add beyond the boot verse?

steps.title: A nation is punished only when it is sent away
steps.stepSummary: The verse teaches רב חיננא בר פפא's rule: the הקב"ה punishes a nation only at the time it is sent away.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches what רב חיננא בר פפא said: the הקב"ה does not punish a nation until the time it is sent away, as it says 'in full measure, when you send her away.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the third פסוק teaches when a nation is punished: only at the very end, when it is 'sent away.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The important words are 'בְּשַׁלְּחָהּ', 'when you send her away.' רב חיננא בר פפא reads them as a time limit: the הקב"ה waits and collects a nation's punishment all at once at its final end. This is new, so the verse is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: The time it is sent away, meaning its final end

phrases.english: It teaches what Rav Ḥinnana bar Pappa said.
For Rav Ḥinnana bar Pappa said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נִפְרָע מִן הָאוּמָּה
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, does not punish a nation
until the time it is sent away,
phrases.notes: He means the nation's final end, when it is wiped out.

phrases.english: as it says: "In full measure, when you send her away, etc."

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The verse teaches that a nation is punished only at the time of its final sending away.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer creates a clear rule about timing, and the next step will test that rule.

steps.title: Egypt was punished more than once
steps.stepSummary: רבא says Egypt drinks three separate cups of punishment, which seems to clash with punishment only at the end.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבא said: why are three cups mentioned about Egypt? One it drank in the days of משה, one it drank in the days of פרעה נכה, and one it will drink in the future with the other nations!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב חיננא בר פפא's rule using רבא's teaching about Egypt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חיננא בר פפא said a nation is punished only once, at its end. But רבא counts three different times Egypt is punished, and Egypt still exists after the first two. So it seems a nation can be punished before its final end.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say? (brings a source that seems to clash)
Cups, here meaning portions of punishment
A later king of Egypt who was defeated

steps.confusionAlert: The three cups here are not the four cups of the סדר. They are the cups in the dream of פרעה's butler, which רבא reads as hints to Egypt's future punishments.

phrases.english: Is that so?
But didn't Rava say:
Why are three cups mentioned about Egypt?
phrases.notes: These are the cups in the butler's dream, בראשית 40:11-13. Some versions have the extra letter in round brackets and some don't.

phrases.english: One that it drank in the days of Moses,
and one that it drank in the days of Pharaoh Neco,
and one that it will drink in the future with its companions!
phrases.notes: 'Its companions' means the other nations, punished together in the future.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule taught in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חיננא בר פפא's rule that a nation is punished only at the time it is sent away.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא shows Egypt being punished at several different times while it still exists, so punishment does not wait only for the end.

steps.title: The later Egyptians are still the same Egyptians
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא blocks a possible answer, that the later Egyptians were a different people. It brings a ברייתא showing that in the time of רבי עקיבא, Egyptians were still treated as the Egyptians of the תורה's law.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say those Egyptians are gone and these are different ones, isn't it taught: רבי יהודה said, 'מנימין the Egyptian convert was my friend among the students of רבי עקיבא.' מנימין said: 'I am a first-generation Egyptian and I married a first-generation Egyptian woman. I will marry my son to a second-generation Egyptian woman, so that my grandson will be allowed to enter the קהל.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops a possible answer to רבא's challenge before anyone can use it. It shows from a ברייתא that the Egyptians of later times still counted as the same Egyptians.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone could say Egypt was not really punished more than once, because the later 'Egypt' was a new people. But מנימין, living long after the exodus, still kept the תורה's rule that only the third generation of Egyptian converts may marry into the קהל. That means Egypt was still the same nation, so the challenge stands.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say. It brings up a possible answer, usually to reject it.
But isn't it taught in a ברייתא? It brings a source to push back.
To enter the congregation, meaning to marry into the Jewish people.

steps.confusionAlert: This step is not a new topic about converts. The story of מנימין is only brought to prove that Egypt in later times was still the same nation, which keeps רבא's challenge alive.

phrases.english: And if you will say: those have gone
phrases.notes: He means the original Egyptians from the time of the exodus are no longer around.

phrases.english: and these are other ones
but isn't it taught: Rabbi Yehuda said:
Minyamin the Egyptian convert

phrases.aramaic: הָיָה לִי חָבֵר מִתַּלְמִידֵי רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא.
phrases.english: was a friend of mine from among the students of Rabbi Akiva.
Minyamin the Egyptian convert said:
I am a first-generation Egyptian,
and I married a first-generation Egyptian woman.
I will marry off my son to a second-generation Egyptian woman
so that my son's son will be
permitted to enter the congregation!
phrases.notes: The תורה lets Egyptian converts marry into the Jewish people only from the third generation (דברים 23:8-9).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא הָנָךְ אֲזַדוּ וְהָנֵי אַחֲרִינֵי נִינְהוּ — וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the challenge of step 10 by shutting down a possible answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible answer that the later Egypt was a different nation, so רב חיננא בר פפא's rule is not broken.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: מנימין still kept the Egyptian third-generation rule in the days of רבי עקיבא, so later Egyptians were the same nation. Egypt was therefore punished more than once, against the rule of punishing only at the end.

steps.title: רב חיננא בר פפא's rule is really about a king
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rewords רב חיננא בר פפא's statement: הקב"ה delays punishing a king, not a nation, until the king is sent away.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said: רב חיננא בר פפא said, הקב"ה does not punish a king until the time he is sent away, as it says, 'In full measure, when you send her away, you contend with her.'
steps.whatsHappening: Since the challenge could not be answered, the גמרא changes the wording of רב חיננא בר פפא's rule. Now it is about a king and not about a whole nation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the rule said a nation is punished only when it is sent away, and Egypt's three cups clashed with that. Now the rule is limited to an individual king, whose punishment waits until he is removed. A nation like Egypt can be punished several times without any problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said. It fixes the wording of an earlier statement.
The time he is sent away, removed from his position

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common גמרא move: when a statement runs into a strong challenge, the גמרא may say it was really said in a narrower way.

phrases.english: Rather, if it was stated, it was stated like this:
Rav Chinnana bar Pappa said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נִפְרָע מִן הַמֶּלֶךְ
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, does not punish a king
until the time he is sent away,
as it is stated: "In full measure, when you send her away, you contend with her" and so on.
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 27:8

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 10-11 by narrowing רב חיננא בר פפא's rule.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rewording the statement so it applies more narrowly
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב חיננא בר פפא's rule was about a nation, which clashes with Egypt being punished three times.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule is about a king, who is punished only when removed, so a nation can be punished more than once.

steps.title: אמימר's version: הקב"ה does not strike a nation twice
steps.stepSummary: אמימר places רב חיננא בר פפא's teaching on a פסוק in מלאכי: הקב"ה strikes a nation once and does not need to repeat it, while בני ישראל are struck many times and never wiped out.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר taught רב חיננא בר פפא's statement on this: What does it mean, 'For I, ה׳, have not changed, and you, sons of יעקב, are not consumed'? 'I, ה׳, have not changed' means I did not strike a nation and then strike it a second time. 'And you, sons of יעקב, are not consumed' is what is written, 'I will use up My arrows on them.' My arrows are used up, but they are not used up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different version of where רב חיננא בר פפא's teaching was said. In this version it explains a פסוק in מלאכי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word שניתי ('changed') is read as 'repeated': when הקב"ה strikes a nation, one blow is enough and He never strikes it again. בני ישראל are the opposite. They are struck again and again, but הקב"ה's arrows run out before they do.

keyTerms.meaning: Teaches, presents a teaching in a certain way
On this, attached to this source
I have not changed, read here as 'I did not repeat'

steps.whatToRemember: A nation is struck once and does not get a second blow, but בני ישראל can be struck many times and are never destroyed.

phrases.aramaic: אַמֵּימָר מַתְנֵי לְהָא דְּרַב חִינָּנָא בַּר פָּפָּא אַהָא,
phrases.english: Ameimar teaches this statement of Rav Chinnana bar Pappa on this:
What is that which is written:
"For I, ה׳, have not changed,
and you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed"?
phrases.notes: מלאכי 3:6

phrases.english: "I, ה׳, have not changed" means:
I did not strike a nation and then strike it a second time.
phrases.notes: The word שניתי can mean 'changed' or 'did a second time.' The גמרא reads it the second way.

phrases.english: "And you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed"
this is what is written: "I will use up My arrows on them."
phrases.notes: דברים 32:23

phrases.english: My arrows are used up, but they are not used up.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמֵּימָר מַתְנֵי לְהָא דְּרַב חִינָּנָא בַּר פָּפָּא אַהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of where and how רב חיננא בר פפא's teaching was said.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הקב"ה strikes a nation one decisive time, while בני ישראל survive many blows.

steps.title: A person is punished only when his measure is full
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא teaches that הקב"ה waits to punish a person until his measure of sin is full.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב המנונא said: הקב"ה does not punish a person until his measure is filled, as it says, 'In the fullness of his plenty he will be in trouble.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching, now about an individual person. הקב"ה waits until the person's sins reach their full measure before punishing him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier steps spoke about nations and kings. רב המנונא applies the idea of waiting to every person. Punishment comes only once the 'סאה', his full measure of sin, is filled, and he learns this from a פסוק in איוב.

keyTerms.meaning: Until his measure is filled. A סאה is a measuring container.

phrases.english: Rav Hamnuna said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נִפְרָע מִן הָאָדָם
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, does not punish a person
until his measure is filled,
as it is stated: "In the fullness of his plenty he will be in trouble" and so on.
phrases.notes: איוב 20:22

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הַמְנוּנָא: אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נִפְרָע מִן הָאָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a related teaching about waiting before punishment, this time for an individual person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person is punished only once his measure of sin is full.

steps.title: A home of praise: משה and דוד
steps.stepSummary: רב חיננא בר פפא reads 'נאוה תהלה' as 'נוה תהלה', a home of praise, and says it refers to משה and דוד, whose enemies never took control of their works.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חיננא בר פפא explained a פסוק: 'Sing joyfully, righteous ones, in ה׳; for the upright, praise is fitting.' Don't read it as 'praise is fitting.' Read it as 'a home of praise.' This means משה and דוד, because their enemies never got control over what they built.
steps.whatsHappening: Because the גמרא just quoted רב חיננא בר פפא, it now brings another one of his teachings. He reads a word in a פסוק with different vowels to find a hidden message.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word נאוה ('fitting') is read as נוה ('a home'). So the פסוק is about the 'homes' that righteous people built for הקב״ה. משה built the משכן and דוד built the gates, and enemies never captured what they made. The next step shows how each one was protected.

keyTerms.meaning: Explained a פסוק to bring out a deeper lesson
'Don't read it as…': reading the same letters with different vowels to teach something

steps.confusionAlert: 'אל תקרי' does not mean the פסוק is spelled wrong. The simple meaning stays. The second reading adds an extra lesson.

phrases.english: Rav Chinena bar Pappa expounded:
What is meant by what is written:
"Sing joyfully, righteous ones, in ה׳;
for the upright, praise is fitting"?
phrases.notes: תהלים 33:1

phrases.english: Do not read it as "praise is fitting,"
but rather as "a home of praise."
phrases.notes: Almost the same letters with different vowels: נאוה means 'fitting,' and נוה means 'a home.'

phrases.english: This refers to Moshe and David,
whose enemies did not gain control over their works.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּרֵשׁ רַב חִינָּנָא בַּר פָּפָּא, מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings another teaching from רב חיננא בר פפא, whose words were just discussed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'נוה תהלה' refers to משה and דוד, whose works were never captured by their enemies.

steps.title: How דוד's gates and משה's משכן were protected
steps.stepSummary: דוד's gates sank into the ground. משה's אהל מועד and all its parts were hidden away once the first מקדש was built.
steps.simpleTranslation: For דוד, the פסוק says: 'Her gates sank into the ground.' For משה, a teacher said: once the first מקדש was built, the אהל מועד was hidden away, with its boards, clasps, bars, pillars and sockets.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the דרשה by showing, for each of the two, how their work escaped the enemy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Jerusalem was destroyed, but the gates דוד made did not fall into enemy hands, because they sank into the ground. The משכן משה built was never captured either, because it was hidden away before any destruction came.

keyTerms.meaning: The Tent of Meeting, which is the משכן
Its boards and its clasps (parts of the משכן)

phrases.english: David: as it is written:
"Her gates sank into the ground."
phrases.notes: איכה 2:9

phrases.english: Moshe: as the Master said:
Once the First Temple was built,
the Tent of Meeting was hidden away,
its boards, its clasps, and its bars,
and its pillars and its sockets.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the claim in step 15 is true for both דוד and משה.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that enemies never controlled the works of משה and דוד.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק in איכה for דוד, and a teaching ('אמר מר') about hiding the אהל מועד for משה.

steps.title: Where was the Mishkan hidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where the אהל מועד was hidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short follow-up question: where exactly was the משכן put away? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teaching said the אהל מועד was hidden but did not say where. The גמרא wants that missing detail.

phrases.english: Where?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a detail left out of the teaching in step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The location where the אהל מועד was stored.

steps.title: Under the tunnels of the היכל
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא, quoting אבימי, says the אהל מועד was hidden beneath the tunnels of the היכל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of אבימי: under the tunnels of the היכל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the משכן was stored underground, beneath the היכל of the מקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משכן was kept in hidden tunnels under the holiest building. That is why no enemy ever got hold of it.

keyTerms.meaning: The main sanctuary building of the בית המקדש

steps.whatToRemember: משה's משכן and דוד's gates were never captured. The משכן was hidden under the היכל, and the gates sank into the ground.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said in the name of Avimi:
Beneath the tunnels of the Heichal.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Under the tunnels of the היכל.

steps.title: Wanting what is not yours makes you lose what you have
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: the סוטה wanted someone not fit for her. She does not get him, and she also loses her husband. The same is true for anyone who wants what is not his.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: a סוטה set her eyes on someone who was not fit for her. What she wanted, she did not get. What she already had was taken from her. This is true for everyone: whoever sets his eyes on what is not his does not get what he wants, and loses what he has.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the topic of סוטה and brings a ברייתא with a moral lesson about her punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סוטה reached for another man. She ends up forbidden to him, and she also loses her own husband. The ברייתא turns this into a general rule: chasing what is not yours costs you even what is yours.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman suspected of being unfaithful to her husband
What is already in her hand, what she already has

steps.whatToRemember: Whoever reaches for what is not theirs loses both: they don't get what they wanted, and they lose what they had.
steps.whyThisMatters: This opens a set of teachings showing that a person who wants what belongs to someone else ends up losing what is already his.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A sotah set her eyes
on one who is not fit for her;
what she wanted was not given to her,
phrases.notes: She becomes forbidden to the other man.

phrases.english: and what she had in her hand was taken from her.
phrases.notes: This means her own husband, who is now forbidden to her too.

phrases.english: For anyone who sets his eyes
on what is not his,
what he wants is not given to him,
and what he has is taken from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: סוֹטָה נָתְנָה עֵינֶיהָ בְּמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ רָאוּי לָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side discussion about רב חיננא בר פפא and returns to the main topic of סוטה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whoever sets his eyes on what is not his does not get it, and loses what he already has.
